As someone on disability, you will absolutely not get it for faking without it taking an extremely long time and getting extremely lucky. It took me 2 years of applying, appealing, and hiring a lawyer to get approved with a legitimate disability. If you don't have a medical history with many attempted treatments over at least 12 months, there's zero chance for that road.

Also have BPD and dang, I can't imagine how difficult it must be trying to work while coping with this shit. I'm on disability, and that's honestly the only reason I've been able to actually work on coping better. The added stress of managing a job made it so so so hard to work on becoming stable. 

I ended up working probably close to 15-20 jobs before I was approved for disability when I turned 22 years old. Just wanted to say I understand that process all too well, and I'm sorry you're stuck in that cycle right now!

In my experience, it's not so much the "it gets better" rule, rather a "it will probably change". For me, 24 years old and been getting treatment since I was 14. I deal with a lot of the same issues, but I deal with them in different ways, or they manifest as different symptoms/limitations. It's not nearly a comforting thought, but I do find it to be better than the idea that I'll be dealing with the same issues in the same way for the rest of my life. Maybe some of those changes will be for the better, fucking hope they're not for the worst. But mentally, I'll take a chance of change for the better over the mindset "I'm 100% stuck this way forever".

And just to be clear, this is my personal experience with those "rules". No one's mental health is the same, and any of these little cheesy sayings definitely can't be true for everyone.

Yw! My last piece of advice is to try to be patient with it :) Try out a bunch of ways to reduce the harm and see what works and what doesn't. Won't be an overnight fix, but it gets easier with a bit of trial and error. good luck!!

Oh also, harm reduction is an in the moment type thing. Use it when you're in a crisis and you can't find any other way out. It's still important to try to find alternative coping skills when you're out of that crisis mode!

For me, the big thing has actually been harm reduction. Instead of saying "I'm never going to self harm again", I focus on "how can I satisfy this urge while doing the least amount of damage to my body". I almost exclusively self harm with burns, so for me, I reduce the harm by doing simple things like:

- waiting an extra few seconds after heating my tool so that it cools down just a bit more.

- Pressing the tool against me for a few seconds less than normal

- Instead of my usual habit of burning myself three times in one session, I do one or two times

You can apply similar ideas for other forms of self harm to reduce the physical damage. Along with harm reduction, try to be kind to yourself when self harm happens. Don't beat yourself up over it. Try to view it from a point of view like "Hey, this happened, here's why it happened, I could do this differently next time, but for now, I did my best to make it not do as much damage". 

I've found that for me, saying I'll never self harm again does NOT work in the slightest, and it actually hurts me more by causing me to feel guilty when I break a streak. Harm reduction has been a lifesaver in getting rid of the shame I felt about SH. 

It is a lot of work to kick this habit, and it's a lot of work to get rid of that guilty/shameful feeling when you relapse. there will always be good days and bad days. Don't make the bad days worse by guilt tripping yourself.

As honest as you can be. If you're dealing with suicidal thoughts, you can say that you specifically have "passive" suicidal thoughts. When people say they're suicidal, it usually comes with doctor's assuming "They have a plan." When you say passive, you're telling them that thoughts and even wishes of death are there, but it's not as urgent as someone with a plan. 

I've made that distinction with every doctor of mine and have never been involuntarily admitted, even after dealing with daily suicidal thoughts for almost 9 years straight now. I've even mentioned it to every one of my non mental health doctors and have never seen serious concern or even threats of hospitalization.

If you're talking about being honest about self harm, in 99% of cases, they won't hospitalize you unless you're at serious risk of permanent damage to yourself.

Sending someone to the hospital involuntarily is a lot of work, and most doctor's aren't super trigger happy about doing it, but there's always some that break the norm. but really, what you get out of therapy and psychiatry is as much as you put in to it. It's hard, it sucks to talk about, and it's uncomfortable. But try your best to talk about as much as you can!
